title: World Cinema Radar — the podcast, Thursday 5 November 2026

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to World Cinema Radar, the podcast. I'm {A}, and it's Thursday the fifth of November.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And I'm {B}. <chuckle> A quieter morning for headlines, but a good one for what you can actually watch this weekend.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Right. Three big things today. First, the Tokyo International Film Festival closed yesterday, and we have the full list of winners.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Second, Friday on Filmin in Spain. A film about one of the greatest stage actresses of all time lands there, and it fits this show perfectly.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And third, opera in cinemas. The Royal Ballet and Opera has a Carmen coming on the tenth. <short pause> With a catch about Spain.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: As always, everything we say is in the written edition, with sources and dates. And where the sources disagree, we say so.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: We also keep the usual rule. Confirmed things are separated from provisional ones, and we don't say a film is available in Spain unless a source says so.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And no spoilers, of course. <chuckle> Not that there is much to spoil today.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Which happens today, a couple of times. <chuckle> Let's start in Tokyo.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So, Tokyo. The thirty-ninth edition finished on Wednesday evening, and the top prize, the Tokyo Grand Prix, went to "Sister Brother Manhole Cover", by Milcho Manchevski.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Manchevski. And that is a very international result, because it's a co-production of six countries: North Macedonia, Bulgaria, Serbia, Albania, Italy and the United Kingdom.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Producer Jane Kortoshev accepted the prize on his behalf. Which means the director wasn't on stage, but the film got the biggest moment of the night.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Six countries. That's a very Balkan way to make a film. <laugh> What's it about, without spoilers?

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Trade coverage describes two orphaned siblings who make a living stealing manhole covers and bronze statues of national heroes. And the jury praised what they called a seamless blend of humour, tragedy and drama.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Okay, that already sounds like my kind of thing. A dark comedy with a social edge. But let's be honest, we haven't seen it, and we found no review.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Exactly. So it's a title to watch, not one to recommend yet. And there's no Spanish release date that we can verify.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Now the rest of the competition. The Special Jury Prize went to "Magic Atlas", from Singapore, directed by Sun Xun.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And best director went to Lisandro Alonso, for "Double Freedom". It's a co-production between Chile, Argentina, Luxembourg, Germany and the United Kingdom.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Alonso is the kind of director whose films you never forget, even if you can't explain them. Good news for him.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The acting awards. Best actress is Hu Ling, for "The Night That Binds Us", a France and Hong Kong film. And best actor is Narita Ryo, for "Two Cigarettes, Three Nights", from Japan.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: His director, Mishima Yukiko, went up to collect it for him. Then best artistic contribution went to "Until the Day Ends", by Jelena Maksimović, for its cinematography.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the Audience Award is "Heysel 85", by Teodora Ana Mihai.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: There are also the side sections. In Asian Future, the best film is "Serife Tavsan", by Tareq Daoud. <short pause> And here's one of our disagreements.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Yes. The festival's winners page prints that title as if it were the director's name. The ceremony report gives the title properly, so that's the one we follow.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Always check the second page. <chuckle> And in Nippon Cinema Now, the best film is "silver express", by Tanaka Miki.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: One more thing I liked. The Kurosawa Akira Award, which comes with a million yen for each winner, went to two directors: O Mipo from Japan, and Mohammad Rasoulof from Iran.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Rasoulof, whom the committee praised for his uncompromising look at injustice and oppression.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Presented the night before the closing ceremony, at the Imperial Hotel. So, summary: nothing here has a verified Spanish date yet, but the list is a good map of what might show up at festivals in the next months.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: One thing worth saying about all these names. Many of these films come from places that rarely reach a Spanish cinema: Singapore, the Balkans, Japan's independent scene.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Right, and that is exactly why a festival list like this is useful. It tells you which titles to look for if a distributor or a platform picks them up later. <breath>

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The edition is careful on that point. It says none of the winning films has a Spanish release date we can verify. So we don't promise anything.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And we won't pretend we've seen them. For the Grand Prix winner, all we have is the official award page, the jury's comment, and the trade description of the story.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Fair. The official pages are the festival's own, and the sales news comes from the trade press. We keep those apart in the sources.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Also, the ceremony was on the fourth of November, at Hulic Hall in Tokyo. Just so the date is clear for the listeners.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And remember, the full list is in the edition, with links to the official festival pages.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now the part I like most today. Filmin, in Spain, on Friday the sixth of November, adds "Duse", by Pietro Marcello. In Spain it appears as "Eleonora Duse, la divina".

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Theatre history on screen. <short pause> Remind us who she was.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Eleonora Duse was one of the great Italian stage actresses. The film follows her last years, when she returns to the stage despite her fragile health.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And it has Valeria Bruni-Tedeschi in the lead. With Noémie Merlant as her daughter, Fausto Russo Alesi as the poet D'Annunzio, and Noémie Lvovsky as Sarah Bernhardt.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Sarah Bernhardt. That's a casting that makes you smile already. <chuckle> It's an Italian and French film, from twenty twenty-five, a hundred and twenty-two minutes. It competed in Venice, and it was in the official section at Seminci last year.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: What does the critic say? You have Diego Lerer at Micropsia.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: He says it's melodramatic, so much that it might irritate some viewers. But he finds that it suits the character. The script is classic and conventional, and the film inserts some documentary-style images of the period.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Hm. So the film is on the shoulders of the lead actress.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Yes. And he says the second half is the strongest, when her health, her work and her relationships decline. He finds it relevant because it looks at how art, life and politics mix dangerously.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: For this show, honestly, it ticks a lot of boxes. Theatre, period drama, fascism arriving in the background. We haven't seen it, so the affinity note you'll hear later is based on that review.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A small point on the title, because it can confuse people. In Spain the film appears as "Eleonora Duse, la divina". The original title is simply "Duse".

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Good to know when you search for it. <chuckle> The film is Pietro Marcello's, and it's set after the First World War, when Italy buries its unknown soldier.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That is from the Seminci page. It describes her strained relationship with her daughter, her complicated bond with D'Annunzio, and the rise of fascism in the background.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I like that the film doesn't try to tell her whole life. The critic says that choosing the last years is what makes it coherent.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The same day Filmin also adds "Barrio Triste", the debut of a director known as Stillz, produced by Harmony Korine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Teenagers from the suburbs of Medellín steal a local television camera and wander around the city. There's a bank robbery, and a strange paranormal encounter. And music by Arca.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That sounds either brilliant or a mess. <laugh> And there's a documentary, "Broken English", about Marianne Faithfull, by Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It covers her rise, her records, her addictions, and the relationship with Mick Jagger.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Honestly, a Friday on Filmin with this plus a documentary and a strange debut is a good weekend plan. Three very different moods.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Different moods, yes. One is a melodrama about the theatre, one is a street adventure, and one is a music documentary. <laugh> Something for everybody.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Then the rest of November on Filmin. We won't read all of it, but a few things. On the thirteenth, "L'affaire Bojarski", a postwar Paris story about a master forger.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And on the twenty-seventh, "The Love That Remains", by Hlynur Pálmason. A family drama in Iceland's landscapes. Pálmason is a name to remember.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: There's also "Mala bèstia", the debut of Bàrbara Farré, on the twentieth. A mystery fable, described as heir to "Lazzaro Felice".

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That one I want to know more about. And one more disagreement to mention: the third season of the Danish series "Carmen Curlers".

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: OtrosCines says the twenty-fourth. A MarketingDirecto guide says the tenth. We can't resolve it, so check Filmin directly.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The rest, with dates, is in the edition. Dates are Filmin Spain, and we haven't verified subtitles or how long the titles stay.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now physical media. Criterion has revealed its January twenty twenty-seven slate, according to The Film Stage.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the big name is "Parasite", by Bong Joon-ho, which goes to 4K, an upgrade from the twenty twenty-one edition.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Next to it, "Deliverance", by John Boorman, in a new 4K edition with restored sound. And "Midnight Cowboy" at full resolution for the first time since twenty eighteen.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: On Blu-ray, "Chocolat", by Claire Denis, and "Career Girls", by Mike Leigh. <short pause> Denis's debut feature, the article says.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: My favourite is the box. World Cinema Project, volume six, presented by Martin Scorsese. Four recovered films: from Guinea-Bissau, Brazil, Côte d'Ivoire and Iran.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Names of the directors, quickly. Flora Gomes, Luis Sérgio Person, Timité Bassori and Bahram Beyzai. The titles are in the edition.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It's interesting to see Criterion mixing a modern hit with older classics and a box of rarely seen films.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes. And the World Cinema Project box is the kind of thing that makes a physical collection worth having. It brings back films that were hard to see.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But here's the catch, and it's a big one for listeners in Spain. This is a US edition. The article gives no exact dates and no extras, and we don't know about disc region, Spanish or Catalan subtitles, or distribution in Spain.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So for now, it's an import. <sigh> Check Criterion's site for the details.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now the stage corner. The Royal Ballet and Opera brings "Carmen", by Bizet, to cinemas on the tenth of November.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It's a revival of Damiano Michieletto's production, with Sesto Quatrini conducting, and Ginger Costa-Jackson and Russell Thomas as Carmen and Don José.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And that's what both the distributor, Trafalgar Releasing, and OperaWire say. But there are some caveats, and they matter.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: First, the distributor lists it as available internationally, but doesn't name Spain. And we found no Spanish cinema listing it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Second, neither page says whether it is live or a recorded performance. And they give no runtime, no language and no subtitles.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The production itself is well known. It's Michieletto's staging, which means a strongly directed Carmen, and Sesto Quatrini is in the pit.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But we only say what the pages say. They name the director, the conductor and the two leads. For everything else, you need the cinema.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Third, some UK cinema listings give a different cast. So, if you find a screening near you, check the cast with the venue.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Right. And an important distinction for this section: a cinema screening is not the same as a complete recording you can watch at home. So we don't add a recording record.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: We found no other new complete theatre or opera recording with verified access from Spain today. Honest answer, not an exciting one. <chuckle>

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But if you missed yesterday's edition: "Le Roi d'Ys" expires on OperaVision on Sunday the eighth.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let's do the calendar. All dates are verified today and come from the platform guides we cite. They can change.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Today, Thursday the fifth, in Spain, Max adds a batch of films: "Black Swan", "The Whale", "Jojo Rabbit", "Cocktail", "Constantine" and "The Color of Money".

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Friday the sixth is the big day. On Filmin, "Duse", "Barrio Triste" and "Broken English". On Movistar Plus, "Wuthering Heights". And on Prime Video, "Campus Drivers".

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The Friday cinema releases in Spain are in yesterday's edition, so we won't repeat them. Sunday the eighth, season two of "City of God: The Fight Rages On" on Max.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Saturday the seventh isn't empty either, but the guide mentions mostly documentaries and light films on Movistar Plus, so we skip them here.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Tuesday the tenth, "Carmen" in cinemas, international, with Spain unconfirmed. Wednesday the eleventh, "El cuerpo" on Netflix, and season three of "The Rings of Power" on Prime Video.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Thursday the twelfth, classics on Max, like "1917" and "Little Miss Sunshine". Friday the thirteenth, "L'affaire Bojarski" on Filmin.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And from the nineteenth to the twenty-seventh, the Filmin titles we mentioned, ending with "The Love That Remains".

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Picks. First, "Duse". On Filmin, Friday the sixth, in Spain. Our affinity note is four out of five, medium confidence.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Remember, that is editorial affinity, not a critics' score. And we haven't seen it. We rely on Diego Lerer's review, which highlights the performance and warns about the melodrama.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Why four? Because it's a period drama, about the theatre, with a big performance at the centre. That is close to what this show likes.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And why only medium confidence? Because one review and a synopsis aren't enough. If you watch it this weekend, tell us whether we got it right. <chuckle>

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Second, "Barrio Triste", same day on Filmin. Three out of five, low confidence, because we only have synopses.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And third, Michieletto's "Carmen" on the tenth. Four out of five, if it reaches Spain. <short pause> A big if.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: For the opera lovers, the cinema is the only route for Carmen right now, since we haven't found a complete recording to watch at home.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And if you like the theatre side, it's worth keeping Filmin in mind for the whole month. There are a lot of dates in the calendar.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the reminder: "Le Roi d'Ys" expires on OperaVision this Sunday.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So, the idea of the day. Not many weighty news items, but a clear awards list from Tokyo and a Friday with theatre, period drama and auteur cinema on Filmin.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Also worth saying: it's a day where the sources mostly agree, with two exceptions. The title on the Tokyo winners page, and the date of the third season of "Carmen Curlers".

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Right. And in both cases, the edition tells you what to check. <chuckle> That is the point of the Radar.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: If you only have time for one thing today, make it Filmin on Friday. The rest of the edition is there for when you want more.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And on physical media, we wait for Criterion's exact dates. <chuckle> Thank you for listening.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: See you tomorrow on the Radar.
